anathema: A formal declaration excluding a person or teaching from the Church's communion; from the Greek for “set apart”. Conciliar anathemas condemn propositions and the people who hold them.
apostolic see: A church founded by an apostle. In the West “the Apostolic See” came to mean Rome specifically; in the East several sees (Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and by later tradition Constantinople, via Andrew) claimed apostolic foundation.
apostolic succession: The continuity of bishops from the apostles through ordination and occupancy of a see. Irenaeus (c. 180) used succession lists to guarantee authentic teaching; later theology emphasised sacramental transmission.
autocephaly: “Self-headed”: the status of an Orthodox Church that elects its own primate and governs itself.
azymes: Unleavened bread used for the Eucharist in the Latin (and Armenian) Church; a major issue in 1053–54.
canon: A rule of church discipline issued by a council or recognised authority. Also: the list of books accepted as Scripture. The two senses should not be confused.
catholicos: Title of the head of certain Eastern Churches outside the Roman imperial system: the Church of the East, the Armenian and Georgian Churches, and the Malankara Orthodox Church.
catholic: Originally “universal, whole” (Ignatius, c. 110). Used by the imperial Church of itself from the 4th century (cf. Cunctos populos, 380); later the self-designation of the Church in communion with Rome. Orthodox Churches also confess the Church as “catholic” in the creed.
chalcedonian: Accepting the Definition of Chalcedon (451). Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and most Protestant Churches are Chalcedonian.
church of the east: The Church of the Persian Empire and Asia, self-governing from 410–424, theologically shaped by Theodore of Mopsuestia. Today: Assyrian Church of the East, Ancient Church of the East, and (in communion with Rome) the Chaldean and Syro-Malabar Churches.
communion: Mutual recognition between churches, expressed above all by sharing the Eucharist and commemorating each other's bishops.
conciliarity: Government of the Church through councils or synods of bishops (Greek synodality).
council: An assembly of bishops (also “synod”). An ecumenical council claims authority for the whole Church; see the introduction to Vol. VI.
diptychs: Lists of living and departed bishops commemorated at the Eucharist; inclusion or removal signified communion or its breach.
doctrine: Church teaching. Dogma is doctrine formally defined as binding; theological opinions (theologoumena) are not binding.
dogma: A doctrine formally defined as binding on the faithful by an authority the Church recognises (e.g. an ecumenical council).
dyophysite: “Two-nature”: affirming two natures in Christ after the union. Used of Chalcedonians and, differently, of the Church of the East.
eastern catholic: Churches of Eastern liturgical tradition in full communion with Rome (e.g. Maronite, Melkite, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Chaldean, Syro-Malabar).
ecumenical: From oikoumenē, the inhabited world (i.e. the Roman Empire). In modern usage also: concerning Christian unity.
energies: In Palamite theology, God's uncreated activities, in which he is truly present and participated, distinct from his unknowable essence.
exarch: In the 5th century, the bishop over a civil “diocese” (group of provinces) — the sense of Chalcedon canon 9; later, a delegate of a patriarch.
filioque: Latin, “and the Son”: the Western addition to the Creed of 381 stating that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
henotikon: Emperor Zeno's “instrument of union” (482) attempting to reconcile Chalcedon's opponents by silence about the council.
heresy: From Greek hairesis, “choice, school”. A teaching judged contrary to the Church's faith; distinguished from schism (a break in communion over order rather than doctrine).
homoian: The 4th-century position that the Son is “like” (homoios) the Father, avoiding substance language; the imperial creed of 359–60.
homoiousios: “Of like substance”: a mediating 4th-century formula (Basil of Ancyra).
homoousios: “Of the same substance/being”: the Nicene term (325) for the Son's relation to the Father.
hypostasis: Concrete individual reality; in Trinitarian theology each of the three “persons”; in Chalcedonian Christology the one subject of Christ.
iconoclasm: “Image-breaking”: Byzantine imperial policy against religious images (c. 726/730–787; 815–843).
jurisdiction: Governing power over a territory or body of faithful (to ordain, judge, legislate), distinct from honour or precedence.
latrocinium: “Robbery”, “robber council”: Leo I's name for the Council of Ephesus of 449.
melkite: From Syriac malkā, “king”: Chalcedonian (imperial) Christians of the Middle East; today also the name of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church.
metropolitan: The bishop of a provincial capital, presiding over the bishops of the province.
miaphysite: “One-nature” (mia physis): the Christology of Cyril's formula as held by the Oriental Orthodox — one united nature of the incarnate Word, without confusion or loss of humanity.
monophysite: Older (often polemical) term for opponents of Chalcedon; in strict use, the Eutychian view that Christ has only a divine nature. Avoided for the Oriental Orthodox, who reject it.
monothelitism: The 7th-century doctrine of one will in Christ, condemned in 681. Monenergism: one “activity”.
nestorian: Polemical term for the teaching that Christ is two persons, attributed to Nestorius; historically misapplied to the Church of the East.
oriental orthodox: The communion of Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara Orthodox Churches, which accept three councils and reject Chalcedon.
orthodox: “Right belief / right glory”. Claimed by all parties; now the self-designation of the Eastern Orthodox (Chalcedonian, Byzantine-tradition) Churches and of the Oriental Orthodox.
ousia: Being, essence, substance: the one divine nature shared by Father, Son and Spirit.
patriarch: Title of the heads of the major sees (from the 5th–6th century); now used by several Churches.
pentarchy: The Byzantine theory of church government by the five patriarchates of Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem.
physis: Nature. Ambiguous in the 5th century: for Cyril often a concrete individual; for Chalcedon the set of properties of divinity or humanity.
pneumatomachians: “Spirit-fighters”: those who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit (later called Macedonians).
pope: “Father”. Used in the 3rd–4th centuries of the bishop of Alexandria (Arius calls Alexander “the Pope”) and of others; in the West from the 6th century increasingly reserved to the bishop of Rome. The Coptic patriarch is still “Pope of Alexandria”.
primacy: First place among bishops or churches. Its content — honour, appellate authority, jurisdiction — is the central disputed question between Catholics and Orthodox.
prosopon: Face, presentation, person; used by Antiochene theologians of the one “person of union” in Christ.
qnoma: Syriac term in the Church of the East's Christology (“two qnome”), best understood as an individuated nature, not a person.
reception: The process by which the Churches accept (or reject) a council's decisions as authentic expressions of the faith.
sabellianism: Modalism: the view that Father, Son and Spirit are modes or roles of one divine person (after Sabellius, 3rd century).
schism: A break in communion, typically over authority or discipline rather than doctrine — though the two are often intertwined.
see: A bishop's seat (Latin sedes) and, by extension, his diocese.
subordinationism: Theologies ranking the Son (and Spirit) below the Father in divinity or being; widespread before Nicaea.
supremacy: Universal jurisdiction over all churches and faithful, as defined for the pope at Vatican I (1870).
synod: A council of bishops. The “home synod” (synodos endemousa) of Constantinople was a standing synod of bishops present in the capital.
theosis: Deification: salvation as participation in the divine life (2 Pet. 1:4), central to Eastern theology and present in Western.
theotokos: “God-bearer”: title of Mary affirmed at Ephesus (431), a statement that the one born of her is God the Word.
three chapters: The person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, writings of Theodoret against Cyril, and a letter of Ibas of Edessa — condemned by Justinian and in 553.
uniatism: Pejorative Orthodox term for the method of bringing parts of Eastern Churches into union with Rome; renounced as a method at Balamand (1993).
messiah: Hebrew mashiach, “anointed one” (Greek Christos): originally a king or priest anointed with oil; in Second Temple texts, various expected agents of God's deliverance.
septuagint: The Greek translation of the Jewish scriptures made in Alexandria (3rd–1st c. BC), abbreviated LXX; the Old Testament of the early Church.
pharisees: A Second Temple Jewish movement devoted to precise interpretation of the Torah and to ancestral traditions; believed in resurrection.
sadducees: Second Temple Jewish party linked to the priestly aristocracy; accepted only the written Torah; rejected resurrection.
essenes: Ascetic Jewish communities described by Josephus, Philo and Pliny; usually linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls community.
apocalyptic: Literature and worldview of revealed secrets about the end of the age, cosmic conflict and judgement (e.g. Daniel, 1 Enoch, Revelation).
diaspora: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel.
logos: Greek “word, reason”: in Stoicism the rational order of the cosmos; in Philo God's agent; in John 1 and the apologists the pre-existent Son.
synoptic gospels: Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be “seen together” because of their shared material.
q: A hypothetical lost source of sayings of Jesus used by Matthew and Luke (from German Quelle, source).
apostolic fathers: Modern label for the earliest non-canonical Christian writings (1 Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, Hermas, etc.).
apologists: Second- and third-century authors who defended Christianity to outsiders (Justin, Athenagoras, Tertullian, etc.).
gnosticism: Modern umbrella term for 2nd-century movements offering saving knowledge and distinguishing the true God from the world's creator; its usefulness is debated.
marcionism: The church founded by Marcion (c. 144), which rejected the Old Testament God and scriptures.
montanism: The “New Prophecy” of Montanus, Prisca and Maximilla (Phrygia, c. 160s–170s), claiming new revelations of the Spirit.
monarchianism: Third-century theologies safeguarding God's oneness either by making the Son a mode of the Father (modalism) or a man adopted by God (adoptionism).
rule of faith: Regula fidei: a summary of essential Christian belief cited by Irenaeus and Tertullian; a forerunner of creeds.
lapsi: Christians who sacrificed or obtained certificates during persecution (especially under Decius, 250).
catechumen: A person under instruction preparing for baptism.
deuterocanonical: Old Testament books in the Septuagint but not the Hebrew canon (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees…); canonical for Catholics and Orthodox, “Apocrypha” for most Protestants.
apocrypha: (1) For Protestants, the deuterocanonical books; (2) non-canonical early Christian gospels, acts and apocalypses.
eucharist: “Thanksgiving”: the Lord's Supper, the central Christian rite of bread and wine.
hellenists: In Acts, Greek-speaking Jewish believers in Jerusalem (Stephen, Philip).
episcopos: Greek “overseer”, origin of “bishop”. In the New Testament overlapping with “presbyter” (elder); by the 2nd century the single leader of a local church.
indulgence: In Catholic teaching, remission of temporal punishment for sins already forgiven; its abuse sparked the Reformation.
scholasticism: The method of the medieval schools: questions, authorities, objections and reasoned resolution.
conciliarism: The view that a general council holds authority superior to the pope (Constance, Haec sancta, 1415).
investiture: Conferral of office; the 11th–12th-century conflict over lay investiture of bishops.
mendicants: “Begging” orders of friars (Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, Augustinians) founded in the 13th century.
inquisition: Judicial procedures against heresy — episcopal, papal, Spanish, Portuguese and Roman forms differed greatly.
sola scriptura: “Scripture alone” as the supreme norm of doctrine (Protestant principle).
sola fide: “Faith alone”: justification by faith apart from works (Lutheran and Reformed).
transubstantiation: Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood (Lateran IV 1215; Trent).
anabaptists: “Re-baptisers”: radical reformers practising believers' baptism (Swiss Brethren, Mennonites, Hutterites).
puritans: English Protestants seeking further reform of the Church of England (16th–17th c.).
ultramontanism: 19th-century movement strengthening papal authority “beyond the mountains” (Rome).
pietism: Lutheran renewal movement stressing personal faith and practice (Spener, Francke).
evangelicalism: Transdenominational Protestant movement marked by conversion, the Bible, the cross and activism.
pentecostalism: Movement from 1901–06 stressing baptism in the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts.
old believers: Russian Orthodox who rejected Nikon's 17th-century liturgical reforms.
millet: Ottoman term for a recognised religious community administered through its leaders.
dhimmi: Protected non-Muslim subject under Islamic law, paying jizya and subject to restrictions.
maronite: Catholic Church of Syriac-Antiochene tradition, named after the hermit Maron; centred in Lebanon.
magisterium: The teaching authority of the Catholic Church (pope and bishops).
liberation theology: Latin American theology from the late 1960s emphasising God's preferential option for the poor.
arminianism: Theology of Jacobus Arminius (d. 1609): resistible grace and conditional election; adopted by Methodists.
adventism: Movements expecting Christ's imminent return; especially the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863).
ordinance: Term preferred by Baptists and others for baptism and the Lord's Supper, viewed as commanded acts rather than means of grace.

doc: Supported by contemporary or near-contemporary sources whose authenticity is not seriously disputed.
con: An inference accepted by a clear majority of specialists, though the sources leave room for argument.
dis: Qualified historians actively disagree; the positions are summarised in the text.
trad: An account preserved within a Church's tradition that cannot be independently confirmed from early sources. This is not a judgement that it is false.
dogma: Officially taught by a Church; reported as that Church's teaching, not as a historical finding.
leg: First attested long after the events it describes.
unc: The evidence is too thin for a confident conclusion either way.

places.t: Apostolic see associated by early tradition with Peter and Paul. First in honour in every first-millennium ranking; seat of the Lateran synods (649) and later Western councils.
Refounded by Constantine in 324–330 as the new imperial capital. Ranked second by canon 3 of 381 and canon 28 of 451. Councils of 381, 553, 680–81, 691–92, 869–70 and 879–80.

Second see of the empire until 381. Home of Arius, Athanasius, Cyril and Dioscorus. After 451 the line of the Coptic popes and a separate Chalcedonian (Melkite) patriarchate both claim its succession.
Where the disciples were first called "Christians" (Acts 11:26); base of Paul's mission; see of Ignatius. Recognised by Nicaea canon 6. Today five Churches claim its patriarchal title.

Site of the Temple, of Jesus' crucifixion and of the first Christian community; destroyed in 70 and refounded as Aelia Capitolina after 135. Given a precedence of honour by Nicaea canon 7 and raised to a patriarchate at Chalcedon (451).
Modern İznik. First ecumenical council (325) and seventh (787). Pope Leo XIV and Patriarch Bartholomew marked the 1700th anniversary here on 28 November 2025.
Council of 431 (Theotokos, deposition of Nestorius) and the contested gathering of 449 that Leo called a 'latrocinium'.

Across the Bosporus from Constantinople. Council of 451, whose definition of 'one person in two natures' produced the longest-lasting division of the early Church. (Marker offset slightly for legibility.)
Modern Sofia. Council of c. 343 that split into rival Western and Eastern assemblies; its canons 3–5 on appeals to the bishop of Rome became central to later debates.
Where Constantine and Licinius met in early 313 and agreed the policy known as the 'Edict of Milan'.
Council of 314, summoned by Constantine over the Donatist dispute.
Centre of the North African Church and of the Donatist schism (from 311/312); Cyprian's see in the 250s.
Where Theodosius I issued the law Cunctos populos (380). Seat of a papal vicariate over Eastern Illyricum.
Imperial residence; place of Athanasius' first exile (335–337).
Western imperial capital from 402; seat of the Byzantine exarchate of Italy until 751.
Charlemagne's court. Council of 809 defended the Filioque; Leo III refused to add it to the creed.
Frankish council of 794 that rejected the decisions of Nicaea II on images, working from a faulty Latin translation.
Third Council of Toledo (589), where Visigothic king Reccared renounced Homoian ('Arian') Christianity; the earliest commonly cited conciliar use of the Filioque.
Lugdunum: church of the martyrs of 177 and of Irenaeus; later the Second Council of Lyon (1274), where Byzantine envoys accepted union, repudiated in the East after 1282.
Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438–39): decree of union Laetentur caeli, 6 July 1439. Rejected in the East, formally so by a synod of 1484.
Council of 1098 at which Anselm of Canterbury defended the Filioque before Greek clergy of southern Italy.
Battle of June 1053: the Normans defeated and captured Pope Leo IX, the immediate background to the legation of 1054.
See of Archbishop Leo, whose letter of 1053 attacking Latin use of unleavened bread helped trigger the crisis of 1054.
Capital of Khan Boris of Bulgaria, baptised c. 864–866; the contest between Rome and Constantinople for his Church shaped the Photian crisis.
See of Basil the Great (370–378/9); centre of Cappadocian theology and of Basil's model of monastic life.
One of the great centres of early Egyptian desert monasticism; Coptic monasteries are still active there.
Approximate area of Pachomius' first communal (coenobitic) monasteries in Upper Egypt, from the 320s.
Monastery of St Catherine, built under Justinian (c. 548–565); one of the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monasteries.
See of Theodore (d. 428), the 'Interpreter' of the Church of the East, condemned posthumously in 553.
Modern Şanlıurfa. Cradle of Syriac Christianity; its 'School of the Persians' was closed by Zeno in 489.
Modern Nusaybin. Persian frontier city whose School became the intellectual centre of the Church of the East after 489.
Sasanian capital; seat of the Catholicos of the East and site of the synods of 410, 424 (at nearby Markabta) and 486.
Seat of the Catholicos-Patriarch of the East from the time of Timothy I (780–823). (Marker offset slightly for legibility.)
Armenian synods of 506 and c. 555 that defined the Armenian Church's stance towards Chalcedon.
Traditional seat of the Armenian Catholicos; Armenia's adoption of Christianity is traditionally dated c. 301, with scholarly estimates ranging to c. 314.
Ancient Georgian capital; royal conversion under King Mirian III in the 330s, associated with St Nino.
Capital of the Aksumite kingdom. King Ezana's coins and inscriptions show adoption of Christianity in the mid-4th century; Frumentius was consecrated bishop by Athanasius.
Umayyad capital (661–750). John of Damascus served its administration before becoming a monk at Mar Saba.
Where Urban II preached the First Crusade (November 1095).
